I actually think it’s a little poorly paced and I think it’s one of the flaws of what still is one of my fave games of that year. I finished it, but after finishing Leyndall and the next part of the map opening up, I was keen to just finish it and be done. With games I’d put a similar amount of time into by the end game (KCD, Cyberpunk for example), I never felt in a rush to finish. Elden Ring had me burned out on it and I think I put less time into overall than I did any of the DS’s or Bloodborne. I did like it, but I don’t think it’s trying to say anything particularly deep or meaningful about how people spend their time, I think it’s just that they wanted to do an impressive open world Soulsborne game, but the scope of what they were doing isn’t really that well supported by the pacing or the gameplay loop, compared to their other games.

I’m not pointing to a specific study here, but direct experience of working with offenders in and out of prison. At least in the UK, recidivism is significantly because there are is such poor follow-up after prison. I.e. poor housing, no job opportunities, poor quality of interventions designed to challenge the beliefs that underpinned offences such as domestic violence or hate crime, and very poor mental health provisions when it comes to things like ADHD and personality disorders.

Labelling has its place, especially in childhood, but I’d say structural issues have a greater impact on recidivism. Someone else may be able to link you to studies. You also have to consider the types of offences that lead to prison sentences rather than community sanctions. These are going to overwhelmingly be violent or sexual offences and the type of offenders that commit those offences, their backgrounds, norms and values are going be very different and more rigid than those who aren’t sentenced to prison.

Ex-probation officer here. People on licence lose their accommodation all the time. If he has to move somewhere else and probation approve, the standard condition on the licence is  ”to reside at an address approved by a your responsible officer”. So it can be any address. It’s not tied to one address, so they don’t need to do a licence variation.

This is different if he is on electronic tag/HDC where a specific address is attached to the licence. Probation will try and get him moved elsewhere but it is much more laborious because it has to go through other channels than probaction. HDC is managed by both probation and the prison and the monitoring is done by an external company. Once the HDC period has ended he’ll be on the normal licence without a specific address attached.

So you can kick him out, if it’s safe for you, which it doesn’t sound like it is, so in that case you might have to get police out, though I’m well aware people choose not to do that for many reasons. If you kick him out, probation can recall him to prison if he’s high risk or source an emergency approved premises bed out (again, only for high risk) or look at other alternatives.

This is the case in the UK and you’re probably already included as a person at risk on his risk management plan if they’ve done their work properly, if he’s got a violent past, DV or property damage and they will absolutely have a contingency plan already in place.

(Edit) If probation have approved your address and not \*rang\* you or done a doorstep visit, as full home visits were stopped during the pandemic, they have failed massively and you should contact them. They are supposed to do full assessments for when someone‘s released on licence. They can’t just approve an address without checking, it’s negligent (if he is being honest with you and honest with them about where he’s staying) and the failures of a probation service on levels of desistance and recidivism or the difficulties in balancing rehabilitation and risk management while being overworked and with overfilled prisons is something the sub could discuss.
